sectionTitle: Waves in air, fluids and solids — part 4.6.1.4

specStatements.text: Sound waves can travel through solids causing vibrations in the solid.

Within the ear, sound waves cause the ear drum and other parts to vibrate which causes the sensation of sound. The conversion of sound waves to vibrations of solids works over a limited frequency range. This restricts the limits of human hearing.
• describe, with examples, processes which convert wave disturbances between sound waves and vibrations in solids. Examples may include the effect of sound waves on the ear drum
• explain why such processes only work over a limited frequency range and the relevance of this to human hearing.
Students should know that the range of normal human hearing is from 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

scopeNotes.statement: Examples may include the effect of sound waves on the ear drum
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification offers the ear drum as a permitted example rather than prescribing a list, so the content teaches the conversion process itself and illustrates it only with the ear drum and with everyday transducers of the same kind (a microphone diaphragm, a loudspeaker cone, a solid object such as a metal rail carrying a tap). No anatomy of the ear beyond 'the ear drum and other parts' is taught - the ossicles, cochlea, hair cells and auditory nerve are not named, and nothing is said about nerve impulses or how the brain processes them, because the specification does not require it. Questions are answerable from the physics of wave-to-vibration conversion alone.

concepts.term: Sound wave travelling through a solid
concepts.definition: A sound wave can travel through a solid, not only through air. As it passes, it causes vibrations in the solid itself: the particles of the solid are made to vibrate about their fixed positions and pass the disturbance on to their neighbours, so the wave is carried through the material.
A thin solid membrane inside the ear. A sound wave arriving at the ear drum makes it vibrate, so the ear drum is the point at which a sound wave in air is converted into vibrations of a solid.

Within the ear, sound waves cause the ear drum and other parts to vibrate, and it is this vibration that causes the sensation of sound. If the vibration is not produced, there is no sensation of sound.

The conversion of sound waves to vibrations of solids works only over a limited frequency range: the solid parts involved can be made to vibrate by some frequencies but not by others. Outside that range the wave disturbance is not converted into vibration of the solid.

Because the ear drum and other parts of the ear only convert sound to vibration over a limited frequency range, human hearing has both an upper and a lower frequency limit. The range of normal human hearing is from 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
Frequency is measured in hertz (Hz), the number of waves passing a point each second. One kilohertz (1 kHz) is 1000 Hz, so the upper limit of normal human hearing, 20 kHz, is the same as 20 000 Hz.

concepts.term: Converting sound waves into vibrations of a solid
concepts.definition: A process in which a sound wave in air arrives at a solid and makes that solid vibrate. Examples: sound waves striking the ear drum and making it vibrate; sound waves striking the diaphragm of a microphone and making it vibrate.

concepts.term: Converting vibrations of a solid into sound waves
concepts.definition: The reverse process, in which a vibrating solid disturbs the air next to it and sends out a sound wave. Examples: the cone of a loudspeaker vibrating and producing sound waves in the air; a struck solid object vibrating and producing a sound.

misconceptions.question: Can a sound wave travel through a solid?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Sound waves can travel through solids, causing vibrations in the solid.
misconceptions.misconception: Sound needs air to travel, so a solid such as a wall or a metal rail blocks it completely - any sound you hear must have got round the solid through the air.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet sound first as 'waves in air' and are taught that sound cannot travel through a vacuum. 'Needs a medium' is then compressed to 'needs air', and everyday experience of walls muffling sound reinforces the idea that solids stop sound rather than carry it.
misconceptions.correction: A sound wave needs a material to travel through, and a solid is a material. In a solid the particles are close together and pass the vibration on very readily, which is why a tap at one end of a metal rail is heard clearly at the other end.

misconceptions.question: What is actually moving when sound passes through a solid?
misconceptions.correct: The solid itself vibrates - the sound wave causes vibrations in the solid.
misconceptions.misconception: The sound squeezes through tiny air gaps or pores between the particles of the solid; the solid itself stays still while the sound passes through it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture the wave as a moving object that must find a path, and particle diagrams drawn with spaces between the circles suggest gaps that air could occupy. It also lets them keep the belief that sound only really travels in air.
misconceptions.correction: There is no separate 'sound' passing through gaps. The wave is the vibration: the particles of the solid vibrate about their positions and pass the vibration to their neighbours, so the solid as a whole is set vibrating.

misconceptions.question: What decides whether a sound can be heard at all?
misconceptions.correct: Whether the frequency lies within the range over which the ear converts sound waves into vibrations of solids - for normal hearing, 20 Hz to 20 kHz.
misconceptions.misconception: It is all about loudness: any sound can be heard if you turn it up enough, and sounds you cannot hear are simply too quiet.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Loudness is the everyday variable students control - volume knobs, moving closer, shouting. Amplitude and frequency are easily conflated, so 'cannot hear it' is read as 'not loud enough' rather than 'the wrong frequency to be converted'.
misconceptions.correction: Loudness and frequency are different properties. A 30 kHz sound played at very high volume is still not heard, because the ear drum and other parts of the ear do not convert a wave of that frequency into vibrations at all.

misconceptions.question: The upper limit of normal human hearing is 20 kHz. What is that in hertz?
misconceptions.misconception: 20 kHz is about 2000 Hz - or perhaps 200 000 Hz; the 'k' just means the number is bigger.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The prefix kilo is handled loosely, and students remember the pair of numbers '20 and 20' without securing which unit each carries. Multiplying by 100 or by 10 000 feels no less arbitrary than multiplying by 1000.
misconceptions.correction: Kilo always means one thousand: 20 kHz = 20 x 1000 Hz = 20 000 Hz. The range of normal human hearing is therefore 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz - a factor of a thousand between the two limits.

misconceptions.question: Where do the limits of human hearing come from?
misconceptions.correct: From the conversion of sound waves to vibrations of solids, which only works over a limited frequency range.
misconceptions.misconception: Nothing physically vibrates - the ear turns sound straight into electrical signals, and it is the brain that decides which frequencies get through.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know hearing ends up as something the brain interprets, and biology lessons emphasise nerves and the brain. The physical, mechanical middle step is skipped, so the limit is attributed to the brain rather than to the vibrating solid parts.
misconceptions.correction: The specification's chain is mechanical: sound waves cause the ear drum and other parts to vibrate, and that vibration causes the sensation of sound. Because the conversion into vibrations of solids only works over a limited frequency range, the limits of hearing are set before any signal reaches the brain.

misconceptions.question: Is a 30 kHz wave a sound wave?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. It is a sound wave; it simply lies outside the range over which the human ear can convert sound into vibrations.
misconceptions.misconception: If nobody can hear it, it is not a sound - sound waves only exist between 20 Hz and 20 kHz.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 20 Hz to 20 kHz figures are learned as a fact about sound rather than as a fact about human ears, so the limits of the detector are mistaken for limits of the wave.
misconceptions.correction: 20 Hz to 20 kHz is the range of normal human hearing, not the range of sound. Waves above and below those frequencies are still sound waves and still make solids vibrate; they are just not converted by the human ear.

misconceptions.question: Can the conversion between sound waves and vibrations of solids work in both directions?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Sound waves can make a solid vibrate, and a vibrating solid can produce sound waves.
misconceptions.misconception: The conversion only goes one way: sound waves make solids vibrate, but a vibrating solid cannot make a sound wave.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The ear drum is the example students meet first and it is always used in the sound-to-vibration direction, so the reverse process is never rehearsed - even though loudspeakers and every struck or plucked object are examples of it.
misconceptions.correction: Both directions occur. A microphone diaphragm is set vibrating by sound waves; a loudspeaker cone vibrates and pushes on the air to send out sound waves. The specification asks for processes which convert wave disturbances between sound waves and vibrations in solids - between, so either way.

misconceptions.question: Does human hearing have a lower frequency limit as well as an upper one?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Normal human hearing runs from 20 Hz up to 20 kHz, so there is a limit at each end.
misconceptions.misconception: Only very high frequencies are outside human hearing; low frequencies can always be heard, so there is no lower limit.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The upper limit is the one students hear about - ultrasound, dog whistles, losing high frequencies with age. Very low frequencies are rarely demonstrated, so the 20 Hz end of the range is remembered as a starting point rather than as a genuine limit.
misconceptions.correction: The range is bounded at both ends because the conversion into vibrations of solids fails at both ends. A 15 Hz wave is a sound wave, but it lies below 20 Hz and is outside the range of normal human hearing.

mcqs.stem: A sound wave from a loudspeaker passes through a brick wall and is heard in the next room. What happens inside the wall as the sound passes through it?

options.text: The particles of the brick vibrate, passing the wave through the solid
options.rationale: Sound waves can travel through solids causing vibrations in the solid: each particle vibrates about its position and passes the disturbance on.

options.text: The wave travels through tiny air gaps between the brick particles
options.rationale: A student who thinks sound only really travels in air imagines it threading through spaces rather than setting the solid itself vibrating.

options.text: The wave stops at the wall because sound can only travel in air
options.rationale: 'Sound needs a medium' is remembered as 'sound needs air', so solids are treated as barriers rather than as materials that carry sound.

options.text: The wave is reflected at the surface, so only a faint echo gets through
options.rationale: Over-applies reflection: some sound is reflected at the surface, but that cannot explain sound arriving on the far side of the wall.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes how sound waves cause the sensation of sound in the ear?

options.text: Nerves in the ear respond to the wave without anything vibrating
options.rationale: Chosen by students who jump straight from wave to nerve signal and leave out the mechanical vibration of solid parts.

options.text: Sound waves make the ear drum and other parts of the ear vibrate
options.rationale: This is the process the specification states: within the ear, sound waves cause the ear drum and other parts to vibrate, which causes the sensation of sound.

options.text: The ear drum only vibrates when a sound is loud enough to hear
options.rationale: Substitutes loudness for the actual mechanism; amplitude is the variable students associate with being able to hear.

options.text: The air inside the ear vibrates but the ear drum itself stays still
options.rationale: Keeps the vibration in the air, consistent with the belief that solids do not themselves vibrate when sound reaches them.

mcqs.stem: The cone of a loudspeaker is made to move in and out rapidly and a sound is heard. Which conversion is taking place at the cone?

options.text: Sound waves in the air are converted into vibrations of a solid
options.rationale: Students who have only met the ear drum apply the conversion in the sound-to-solid direction whatever the device.

options.text: Sound waves are converted into electrical signals inside the cone
options.rationale: Reaches for an electrical step because that is how they picture any sound device working, and reverses the direction as well.

options.text: Vibrations of a solid are converted into sound waves in the air
options.rationale: The vibrating cone is a solid that disturbs the air next to it, sending out a sound wave - the solid-to-sound direction of the conversion.

options.text: The cone changes the frequency of the sound waves in the air
options.rationale: Confuses producing a sound with altering one; a plausible choice for students who think a speaker modifies an existing wave.

mcqs.stem: A microphone contains a thin diaphragm. A student speaks into the microphone. What happens at the diaphragm first?

options.text: The diaphragm vibrates first and then creates sound waves
options.rationale: Runs the conversion in the loudspeaker direction, which a student may do if the two devices are not distinguished.

options.text: The sound wave passes through gaps in the diaphragm
options.rationale: Keeps the wave in the air and treats the solid as something to get past rather than something set vibrating.

options.text: The sound is turned into electricity without anything moving
options.rationale: Skips the mechanical step entirely, the same error students make when describing the ear.

options.text: Sound waves in the air make the solid diaphragm vibrate
options.rationale: This is the same conversion as at the ear drum: a sound wave arrives at a solid and sets it vibrating.

mcqs.stem: A signal generator and loudspeaker produce a sound at 30 kHz at very high volume. A student with normal hearing hears nothing. Why?

options.text: The conversion of the wave into vibrations does not work at that frequency
options.rationale: The conversion of sound waves to vibrations of solids works only over a limited frequency range; 30 kHz is above 20 kHz, so the ear's solid parts are not set vibrating.

options.text: The sound is not loud enough for the ear drum to be able to vibrate at all
options.rationale: Attributes inaudibility to amplitude, ignoring that the stem states the volume is very high.

options.text: At 30 kHz the loudspeaker is not producing a sound wave at all
options.rationale: Treats 20 Hz to 20 kHz as the range over which sound exists rather than the range humans hear.

options.text: The ear drum vibrates normally but the brain ignores the signal
options.rationale: Places the limit in the brain instead of in the physical conversion into vibrations of solids.

mcqs.stem: The range of normal human hearing is from 20 Hz to 20 kHz. Written in hertz, what is the upper limit of this range?

options.rationale: Treats the kilo prefix as a factor of 100, a common slip when prefixes are recalled rather than understood.
Over-corrects by a further factor of ten; the student knows the number gets bigger but not by how much.
Multiplies correctly but leaves the unit as kHz, so the answer is a thousand times too large.

mcqs.stem: Which one of these frequencies lies outside the range of normal human hearing?

options.rationale: Picked by students who look only for a high frequency; 12 000 Hz is below 20 000 Hz and is inside the range.
Chosen if 20 kHz has been misremembered as 2000 Hz, making 2000 Hz look like the limit.

options.text: 15 Hz
options.rationale: 15 Hz is below the lower limit of 20 Hz, so it lies outside the range of normal human hearing.

options.text: 300 Hz
options.rationale: Comfortably inside the range; selected by students guessing that mid-range values are unusual.

mcqs.stem: One student taps the far end of a long metal railing. Another student, with an ear against the railing, hears the tap clearly. Which statement explains this?

options.text: Sound cannot travel in metal at all, so it must have come through the air
options.rationale: Holds that sound requires air; the student invents an air path rather than accept a solid one.

options.text: The sound travels through gaps in the metal without moving it
options.rationale: Allows sound into the solid but not the solid to vibrate, preserving the idea that only air carries sound.

options.text: The metal makes the sound louder so it can be heard much further
options.rationale: Confuses efficient transmission with amplification; the railing carries the sound, it does not add energy to it.

options.text: The tap sets the metal vibrating and the vibrations travel along it
options.rationale: Sound waves can travel through solids causing vibrations in the solid, so the railing itself carries the disturbance to the listener.

mcqs.stem: Why does the conversion of sound waves into vibrations of solids only work over a limited frequency range?

options.text: Solid parts such as the ear drum will only vibrate over a limited range
options.rationale: The solid can be set vibrating by some frequencies and not by others, so outside that range no conversion takes place.

options.text: Only sounds above a certain loudness can make any solid vibrate
options.rationale: Replaces a frequency limit with an amplitude limit, the commonest substitution students make here.

options.text: Sound waves only exist over a limited range of frequencies
options.rationale: Turns a limit of the detector into a limit of the wave itself.

options.text: The brain, not the ear, decides which frequencies are converted
options.rationale: Locates the limit after the conversion rather than in it.

mcqs.stem: The ear drum and other parts of the ear can be made to vibrate only within a limited range of frequencies. What does this fact explain?

options.text: Why very quiet sounds cannot be heard at any frequency
options.rationale: Reads a statement about frequency as a statement about loudness.

options.text: Why human hearing has an upper and a lower frequency limit
options.rationale: The restricted conversion sets both ends of the range of normal human hearing, 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

options.text: Why sounds outside human hearing are not really waves
options.rationale: Concludes that unconverted waves are not sound, rather than simply unheard.

options.text: Why hearing has an upper limit but no lower limit at all
options.rationale: Remembers only the 20 kHz end, so the 20 Hz end is not treated as a real limit.
